label: Formulated vitalist spiritual monism and transmutative monads
description: Anne Conway formulated an ontology positing three species of substance: God (immutable), Christ/Logos (mediating), and Creation (a continuous, living spiritual continuum whose individual units undergo perpetual moral and physical transmutation).
historicalContext: Composed in Ragley Hall, Warwickshire, in dialogue with Henry More, Francis Mercury van Helmont, and Quaker and Kabbalistic thought.
dialecticalTension: Rejects the dualistic divide between dead matter and thinking mind, asserting that body is simply solidified spirit.

citations.author: Anne Conway
citations.work: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
citations.quote: Spirit and body are originally one and the same in their first substance, differing only in degrees of subtlety and grossness.

citations.author: Christia Mercer
citations.work: Leibniz's Metaphysics: Its Origins and Development

label: Refuted Cartesian dead matter and mechanical mind-body interaction
description: Conway dedicated Chapter 9 of her Principles to refuting Descartes, demonstrating that if matter were purely dead and inert extension as Descartes claimed, no genuine causal interaction between immaterial soul and material body could ever occur.
historicalContext: The intense debate surrounding Cartesianism within the Cambridge Platonist circle in the 1670s.
dialecticalTension: Solves the Cartesian interaction problem by eliminating dead matter: both mind and body are living spirit at different registers of contraction and expansion.

citations.author: Anne Conway
citations.work: Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
citations.quote: Descartes says that body is mere dead matter, devoid of all life and perception... which philosophy is entirely contrary to the true knowledge of God and nature.

citations.author: Jacqueline Broad
citations.work: Women Philosophers of the Seventeenth Century

label: Refuted Spinozistic pantheism and the conflation of God with creatures
description: Conway directly engaged and attacked Spinoza's monism, arguing that collapsing God and creation into a single substance destroys moral responsibility, the reality of evil, and divine goodness.
historicalContext: Conway read Spinoza's Tractatus Theologico-Politicus and related texts through her collaboration with Francis Mercury van Helmont.
dialecticalTension: Maintains a triadic ontological distinction (God, Mediator, Creation) against Spinoza's univocal single substance (Deus sive Natura).

citations.author: Anne Conway
citations.work: Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy
citations.quote: Spinoza confounds God and creatures together, making of both only one substance; but this contradicts the infinite perfection and transcendence of God.

label: Directly inspired Leibniz's monadological metaphysics and living substance
description: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz read Conway's Principles with great enthusiasm, repeatedly citing the 'Countess of Conway' in his letters and notebooks, adopting her vitalist monism, concept of the monad, and pan-organic worldview.
historicalContext: Van Helmont personally delivered Conway's book to Leibniz in Hanover in 1696, sparking intensive discussions on living substances.
dialecticalTension: Leibniz formalizes Conway's theological-transmutative spiritual units into windowless, mathematically pre-established monads.

citations.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
citations.work: Letter to Thomas Burnett of Kemnay
citations.sectionOrPage: Die philosophischen Schriften von G. W. Leibniz (ed. Gerhardt), III, p. 217
citations.quote: My philosophical views approach somewhat closely those of the late Countess of Conway... who maintained that all things are living and perceptive.
